            },
            indent=2,
        )
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The example deliberately uses a coarse Euler step. The member with rate 0.1 has output values 1, 0.9, 0.81; the member with rate 2 has 1, -1, 1. The latter is flagged even though its final value is positive. In a separate example, a cumulative counter has values 5, 4, 3: every state is positive, but its two negative increments are flagged.

docs.title: Scope and interpretation
docs.text:
These checks inspect the requested output grid, including the initial state. They do not inspect internal accepted substeps, rejected attempts or RK stages. For example, the two Euler updates 1 → -1 → 1 would escape a nonnegativity flag if only the first and last values were requested outputs. A successful output record therefore does not prove positivity throughout a solve, numerical accuracy or physical validity. Use a suitable solver, step size or state representation for the model.

nonnegative_indices selects components on the leading state axis; None checks all components. Use a subset when signed states, such as velocities, can legitimately be negative. Checks apply to the coordinates stored by the solver. For log coordinates or other transformed states, decode the stored trajectory before checking physical-state nonnegativity. monotone_indices selects cumulative components whose output increments should be nonnegative. A model's observation transformation may need separate checks; the solver cannot infer which derived observations should be monotone.

All remaining subgroup and field axes are retained in the diagnostic arrays. A simulation bank can therefore keep a flag per member without collapsing failures across the whole bank. Counts flag each output or interval once if any selected component fails; they do not count failing components.

Field Meaning n_outputs Number of inspected output records, including the initial state complete Every output on the solve's grid was inspected; false for a partial failed run min_state Minimum selected state over those outputs; NaNs propagate n_negative_outputs Output records with any selected state below the negative tolerance n_nonfinite_outputs Output records with any nonfinite component, including unselected components min_increment Minimum selected cumulative increment; None when disabled, positive infinity when no interval exists n_decreasing_intervals Output intervals with a cumulative decrement; None when disabled valid Native flags for a complete, finite record with no threshold violations on the checked outputs

negative_tolerance and monotone_tolerance are finite, nonnegative absolute thresholds. Equality at minus the tolerance is accepted. They change the flags, not the recorded minima or trajectory; no value is clamped or projected. The increment tolerance is an amount per output interval, not a rate scaled by its duration.

docs.title: Storage and backends
docs.text:
The eager driver collects running minima and counts, including when ModelCoreOptions(store_history=False) discards output history. Whole-grid scan drivers reduce diagnostics over their output trajectory with native array operations, rather than unrolling a diagnostic loop. NumPy, JAX and CPU PyTorch have independent count checks; JAX JIT/vmap and state gradients are covered. Flags stay in the state's array namespace; the checks do not extract host scalars inside a compiled solve.

diagnose_trajectory(trajectory, config) performs the same output checks on an existing real floating array shaped (output, state, *other_axes), including stored stochastic paths or provider outputs. It checks the supplied records; the standalone function cannot determine whether a larger solve completed. The core option above applies to CoreSolver; provider prepared runners and stochastic solver configurations have their own interfaces.

Retain these records with the simulation results when choosing how to handle flagged draws. Rejecting parameter draws changes the simulated distribution; use a stated acceptance rule consistently for fitting and calibration.

docs.title: Per-run random streams
docs.text:
The stochastic solvers already accept injected samplers on each run. NumPy states can now use rng= instead: pass a numpy.random.Generator or SeedSequence to DirectSSASolver.run, TauLeapingSolver.run, AdaptiveTauLeapingSolver.run, or ThinningSSASolver.run. This creates local NumPy convenience samplers without rebuilding the solver or changing any independently held sampler.

import numpy as np
from op_engine import DirectSSASolver, ModelCore

core = ModelCore(1, 1, np.array([0.0, 0.5, 1.0]))
initial = np.zeros((1, 1))
core.set_initial_state(initial)
solver = DirectSSASolver(core, np.array([[1.0]]))

def births(t, y):
    return np.full(y.shape, 12.0)

seed = np.random.SeedSequence([3, 7, 2, 2026])
solver.run(births, rng=seed)
first = core.state_array.copy()
core.set_initial_state(initial)
solver.run(births, rng=seed)
assert np.array_equal(core.state_array, first)

Reset the ModelCore with set_initial_state before rerunning it. Resetting state/time/history and resetting random draws are separate operations. A run does not automatically restore initial state or roll back a failing simulation.

docs.title: Stream ownership and compatibility
docs.text:
A supplied Generator is used directly and advances in place. Reusing that object continues its stream, even after resetting model state. Construct a fresh generator from the same recorded initialization to replay. Do not share one mutable generator across concurrent tasks.

A supplied SeedSequence initializes a fresh generator per run. Reusing it replays the same draw stream when the method, model, state, parameters, grid and software stack are identical. The engine does not call spawn or mutate its child counter. Adaptive tau's Poisson and exact-event convenience samplers share one call-local generator, consuming it in the algorithm's draw order.

NumpyPoissonSampler, NumpySSASampler, and NumpyThinningSampler also accept rng=. A sampler constructed from a SeedSequence initializes once and then advances statefully when reused, just like a legacy seeded sampler. Existing Sampler(seed) construction remains valid. An integer seed and rng are mutually exclusive; solver rng accepts only Generator or SeedSequence, not bare integers. Missing samplers/streams and combining rng with explicit sampler(s) raise ValueError before integration. Non-NumPy states reject this convenience path before sampling, including inactive runs.

Existing explicit sampler protocols retain their signatures, native namespaces and draw-index semantics. JAX functional keys or Torch-native sampling belong in those injected samplers. An adaptive run without rng still needs both its Poisson and exact-event samplers; an explicit stream cannot silently replace either one. There is no instance generator on the solver to override: stateful legacy randomness lives in the injected NumPy sampler.

docs.title: Indexed replicates and reproducibility
docs.text:
Use stable, nonnegative identifiers to initialize a stream independently of worker launch order:

stream = np.random.SeedSequence([replicate_id, unit_id, stage_id, root_seed])
core.set_initial_state(initial)
solver.run(births, rng=stream)

Record the identity order and root seed. Distinct replicate/unit/stage identities give different initializations with NumPy's probabilistic stream-independence properties. Fixed allocation trees can alternatively use recorded spawn children. Sequential spawning depends on allocation order; indexed identities make reordered execution straightforward. These schemes follow NumPy's parallel random-stream guidance. The engine delegates PRNG selection and initialization to NumPy; a caller can supply a Generator with its chosen BitGenerator.

Record NumPy/BitGenerator versions and type, method/configuration, output and forcing grids, state layout, model/parameter identity and stream identity with study artifacts. NumPy's default Generator distribution draws do not carry a general cross-version bitwise guarantee; see its compatibility policy. No random source is serialized automatically by this engine interface.

Repeating a stream does not guarantee the same path after changing parameters, methods or adaptive decisions: those can change draw counts/order. Shared seeds alone do not establish event-wise common-random-number coupling, statistical independence, or an exact likelihood target. Such consumer policies remain separate from this per-run numerical interface.

Required NumPy qualification checks same-solver replay, generator advancement, reordered indexed replicates, preservation of existing samplers, conflicting sources and analytic constant-birth endpoint mean/variance. Native JAX/Torch checks verify the NumPy convenience boundary. Existing injected-key JAX tests remain in the baseline stochastic suites; this change adds no new native PRNG implementation or stochastic differentiation claim.

docs.title: Accepted meshes: compatibility and accuracy
docs.text:
A frozen accepted mesh is static controller output. Replay invokes its numerical steps and bypasses adaptive error estimates and acceptance decisions. Its AD results are derivatives conditional on that mesh. A compatible mesh may still become inaccurate when model parameters or initial conditions move.

The core contract distinguishes these questions before testing accuracy:

Metadata Replay treatment Finite/increasing output grid and positive interval steps summing to each interval Always validated by AdaptiveStepSchedule Producing resolved method, state shape/axis order, relevant operator axis, TR-BDF2 gamma, nonlinear stage solver/configuration Known mismatches reject before stepping Declared forcing breakpoints Recorded declarations must match; every accepted step must land at each intervening jump, including legacy/manual meshes Caller-supplied structural model identity Compared when recording/replay use an identity; it must describe equations/geometry/layout, not fitted parameter values Array namespace and dtype Descriptive; portable meshes may change NumPy/JAX/Torch or precision Discovery tolerances, controller limits, and reference parameter regime Descriptive; changing fitted values or requested accuracy requires an external accuracy decision, not an automatic incompatibility Callback bodies and arbitrary custom solver internals No automatic semantic identity guarantee; use the structural identity and independently qualify changed implementations

AdaptiveScheduleProvenance is attached to schedules created by live adaptive runs. RunConfig.replay_model_id and replay_reference_regime are optional static labels supplied by the caller. Record concrete nominal values or a stable parameter-set identifier in the reference label at an eager boundary; replay does not inspect or convert dynamic parameter arrays.

Manually constructed meshes and legacy schedules with provenance=None remain accepted by default after mesh/output-grid validation. Their method/model compatibility is unverified and remains the caller's responsibility. Use RunConfig(replay_require_provenance=True) to reject unverified schedules. Adding a provenance record is not an accuracy certificate, and copying labels from another model does not make that model compatible.

Controller settings are recorded to explain discovery. Replay ignores error control even if the supplied configuration requests tighter tolerances. A provider may impose stronger configuration/context checks on its own artifact; these core rules do not remove those provider checks.

For imex-heun-tr, provenance.discovery_settings also records error_estimator="step-doubling: full-step error", error_estimator_partitions="explicit,implicit", and error_estimator_order="3". These describe the producing controller's cubic local estimate. They are descriptive fields, rather than replay compatibility constraints or accuracy certificates. Older meshes discovered using the explicit-only estimator remain replayable with the same accepted full-step formula, but should be rediscovered and checked independently before reuse where implicit error matters. Replay skips the additional half-step solves.

A practical reuse policy is:

  1. Discover a live mesh at a documented nominal parameter regime.
  2. Reuse it while changing dynamic values, retaining structural model identity.
  3. Compare a replay trajectory to a fresh accurate solve or to a refined mesh at representative new parameter values. Check the scientific objective and needed derivatives as well as state error.
  4. If the independent discrepancy exceeds the intended accuracy, rediscover the mesh at the new regime, recheck agreement, and freeze that mesh for the next differentiation phase.

The structured example accompanying this guide executes that policy and shows an accuracy failure despite compatible provenance. Discrete refresh decisions remain outside the differentiated numerical solve.

Run the structured refresh example:

uv run python examples/replay_mesh_refresh.py

It transfers mass between two generic pools with A'=-k*A^2, B'=+k*A^2, a shared rate and group-local multipliers. The independent solution is A(t)=A0/(1+k*A0*t), with conserved A+B. A mesh discovered at rate 0.05 remains accurate nearby; rate 3.0 is structurally compatible but exceeds the example's 1e-4 state-error policy on the old mesh. Fresh discovery restores that accuracy. JSON reports both discrepancies and accepted-step counts. This policy checks this fixture's state error; different scientific objectives and derivative accuracy need their own independent checks.

docs.title: Independent exact-SSA banks
docs.text:
BatchedDirectSSASolver gives every independent replicate its own event clock. State is (local_species, replicate) and hazards are (local_channel, replicate). One local stoichiometric matrix is shared; no global block matrix expands with bank size. A sweep evaluates hazards once and advances each active replicate by one event or boundary. This avoids reevaluating the entire bank for every event in the superposed DirectSSASolver process.

The first implementation is eager NumPy CPU execution. It supplies no stochastic gradient estimator, accelerator driver, tau-leaping or jump/ODE hybrid mode. Those require separate implementations and qualification.

docs.title: Read a two-replicate simulation
docs.text:
The executable two-replicate example has a numerical illustration:

Replicate ID Initial A Base rate Final A Final B Accepted firings 10 12 0.4 2 10 10 20 17 0.7 0 17 17

Each initial A individual transfers once to B. The base rate is multiplied by one before t = 1 and two thereafter. Thus the analytic mean remaining in A is A(0) * exp(-rate * (min(t, 1) + 2 * max(t - 1, 0))). The smooth curves show the corresponding mean B; markers are observations on the output grid. They do not reconstruct every event time. The two IDs have different initial populations and rates and are not an IID bank for estimating one distribution. The firing ledger agrees with the transferred population in each replicate.

Download the vector PDF. From a checkout, regenerate with:

uv run --with matplotlib==3.11.2 python -m examples.illustrate_replicate_ssa
just figures-check

The source example checks population conservation, firing counts, bank-order invariance and shard replay. figures-check reruns it and checks the generated table, complete plotted data, source identity and export hashes without a plotting dependency. The plotted data retains the numerical inputs.

docs.title: Compile an independent model
docs.text:
With op-system==0.8.0 or later:

import numpy as np
from op_system import compile_spec
from op_engine import (
    BatchedDirectSSASolver, BatchedSSAConfig, FiringRecorder, ModelCore,
    from_compiled_replicates,
)

compiled = compile_spec({
    "kind": "transitions",
    "axes": [{"name": "rep", "coords": ["a", "b"]}],
    "factorize_axes": ["rep"],
    "state": ["S[rep]", "I[rep]"],
    "transitions": [
        {"name": "infect", "from": "S[rep]", "to": "I[rep]", "rate": "beta[rep]"},
        {"name": "recover", "from": "I[rep]", "to": "S[rep]", "rate": "gamma"},
    ],
})
network = from_compiled_replicates(
    compiled, {"beta": np.array([0.2, 0.4]), "gamma": 0.1}, batch_axis="rep"
)
core = ModelCore(2, 2, np.arange(11, dtype=float))
core.set_initial_state(np.array([[90., 70.], [10., 30.]]))
counts = FiringRecorder((0,))
BatchedDirectSSASolver(core, network.stoichiometry).run(
    network.propensity, rng=np.random.SeedSequence(2026), replicate_ids=[8, 19],
    config=BatchedSSAConfig(forcing_breakpoints=network.forcing_breakpoints),
    recorder=counts,
)
trajectory = core.state_array
infection_counts = counts.counts

All evolving templates must carry the certified batch axis. Each reaction must preserve that coordinate and read only its own replicate's state. Shared fixed parameters are allowed. Cross-replicate reductions, routed transfers, omitted reactions, unrepresented operators and missing independence certificates are errors. Shapes alone cannot certify independence. The compiler checks reactions before deterministic cancellation, so cancelling drift is insufficient evidence.

Other local axes, pinned local cells and routed local channels retain the existing compiler conventions. pack_state converts a full compiler flat state to a local bank; flatten_history restores full compiler cell order. The batch axis can occupy any declared template position. Channel names/indices describe local channels, with the replicate dimension separate.

docs.title: Forcing and observations
docs.text:
Hazards must be constant in external time between events and declared forcing changes. The compiled adapter rejects explicit continuous-time dependence and nonconstant linear tables. previous time parameters must explicitly carry the replicate axis, even when the table values are shared across replicates; broadcast those values when constructing the table. This gives the compiler a declared dimension for the different current values at asynchronous clocks.

The adapter selects a table row per replicate and resolves each consumed table once per hazard evaluation. Pass its forcing_breakpoints to the solver config. Generic NumPy callbacks receive the full vector of clocks and can implement shared or per-replicate forcing with forcing_breakpoints and replicate_breakpoints, respectively. Declaring an arbitrary time grid does not make a continuously changing hazard piecewise constant.

Pending events survive pure output boundaries, so refining the output grid does not change a seeded path. A forcing boundary wins a tie and discards the candidate event. A pure output boundary includes an event exactly at that time. Zero rates wait for the next forcing change or remain absorbing. Event limits apply to each replicate in each output interval. Initial counts must be finite, non-negative integers; impossible consumption and non-advancing event times fail explicitly.

The optional FiringRecorder uses the same accepted-event contract as ordinary SSA. Counts are host int64 diagnostics shaped (interval, selected_channel, rep). They consume no random numbers; enabling recording preserves the trajectory.

docs.title: Random streams and replay
docs.text:
A root SeedSequence plus distinct unsigned 64-bit replicate_ids defines native PCG64DXSM streams under versioned scheme OPB1. IDs are framed in the spawn path, not derived by batch-dependent spawn(). Paths replay under reordering, smaller banks and disjoint shards for unchanged inputs and schedules. No cross-version, cross-backend bitwise identity is promised.

Alternatively pass one NumPy Generator/SeedSequence per replicate. Generators advance in place; SeedSequences initialize fresh runs. Duplicate stream states are rejected. The caller owns independence of explicitly supplied streams. An op_infer.rng.RandomKey can supply each simulation SeedSequence without adding an inference dependency to the engine. Common random numbers across designs use the same addresses in separate runs, while each bank retains independent IDs.

Runs replay from their initial state. Mid-trajectory checkpoint/resume with pending-event state is not implemented; a workflow can resume completed replicate artifacts or replay unfinished replicates from their original inputs.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text:
Run the standalone correctness-gated benchmark:

python -m benchmarks.replicate_ssa --sizes 16 64 256 1024 --days 30 \
  --flat-max 64 --output /tmp/replicate-ssa.json

JSON separates compiler/setup/execution costs and records events, sweeps, matrix storage, source identity and environment. The flat comparison is bounded by --flat-max; large superposed banks can be expensive. Timings are not portable thresholds. Required small analytic/replay/compiler/provider tests establish correctness; large measurements remain opt-in. Heterogeneous event workloads can increase sweep counts with bank size, so benchmark the intended parameter bank.

docs.title: Bounded forward parameter sensitivities
docs.text:
solve_sensitivities integrates the smooth deterministic augmented equations S' = (df/dy) @ S + df/dtheta, with S = dy/dtheta. It reuses the existing fixed Euler, Heun, RK4 or DOPRI5 stage equations. This is a numerical approximation to continuous sensitivities; mesh refinement remains necessary.

The engine accepts the structural DerivativeArtifact protocol and imports no compiler or statistical package. The optional op_system.symbolic_derivatives artifact supplies ordered state, parameter and scalar-measurement matrices from one retained source IR. Its own bounded supported-operation contract applies. The caller must bind that artifact to the same RHS and coordinate definitions.

import numpy as np
from op_system import compile_spec, symbolic_derivatives
from op_engine import (
    SensitivityInitial,
    SensitivityOptions,
    SensitivitySystem,
    solve_sensitivities,
)
from op_engine.core_solver import RunConfig

compiled = compile_spec({
    "kind": "expr",
    "state": ["x", "z"],
    "equations": {"x": "-rate*x", "z": "-rate*z"},
    "observables": {"measurement": {"expr": "gain*(x+2*z)"}},
})
system = SensitivitySystem(
    compiled.eval_fn,
    symbolic_derivatives(compiled),
    initial_parameters=("amplitude",),
)
assert system.parameter_names == ("rate", "gain", "amplitude")
solution = solve_sensitivities(
    system,
    {"rate": 0.7, "gain": 1.5, "amplitude": 2.0},
    SensitivityInitial(
        state=np.array([2.0, 4.0]),
        parameter_derivatives=np.array([[0., 0., 1.], [0., 0., 2.]]),
    ),
    np.array([0., 0.5, 1.]),
    options=SensitivityOptions(
        solver=RunConfig(method="rk4", fixed_max_step=0.0625),
    ),
)
assert solution.times == (1.0,)
assert solution.parameter_derivatives.shape == (1, 2, 3)
assert np.allclose(
    solution.observable_derivatives,
    np.exp(-0.7) * np.array([[[-15., 10., 7.5]]]),
    rtol=2e-6,
)

Initial-state derivatives are required. Supply an explicit zero matrix for a parameter-independent initial state. Parameters used only by initialization are appended in initial_parameters order, receive zero RHS/direct-measurement columns, and enter through the supplied initial derivatives. Measurement-only parameters retain their compiler order and direct measurement terms.

For N states, P complete parameters, M scalar measurements and T retained times, the returned native arrays have shapes (T,N), (T,N,P) and (T,M,P). The measured sensitivity is dg/dy @ S + dg/dtheta. A state Jacobian alone does not supply it. Observation noise, prior curvature, experimental design,+nuisance treatment and Fisher definitions belong to inference consumers.

docs.title: Memory and execution scope
docs.text:
The augmented state has N*(1+P) entries. Final-only output is the default; store_history=True retains requested output times, not internal stages. Default bounds are 16,384 augmented entries and 64 MiB of returned numerical arrays. They do not bound temporary work, compiler memory, retained AD graphs or whole-process RSS. The derivative producer may additionally allocate bounded dense matrices at every stage.

State, initial derivatives, native scalar parameters and produced matrices must retain namespace and dtype. NumPy, JAX and CPU Torch float32/64 are qualified. For JAX, close over a static system/mesh/options and return the needed native array fields from the transformed function; the full provenance dataclass is host metadata, not a registered JAX pytree. fixed_loop="scan" and optional checkpointing reuse the existing engine adapter. Independent solves can be batched with native vmap. CUDA requires its own device qualification.

The stored mesh records the solver's actual time dtype. Tolerance settings do not define accuracy for these fixed methods; declare the mesh and maximum step, then check refinement. Adaptive acceptance, forcing jumps, events, history dependence, stochastic models, operator/implicit solves and automatic gauge transformations require separately qualified sensitivity methods. Unsupported solver configurations fail explicitly.

docs.title: Independent checks and cost comparison
docs.text:
Required native backend checks cover independent stability polynomials for all four methods, shared/local states, initial-only parameters, dtype retention, same-mesh finite differences, refinement, JAX JIT/vmap/checkpointing and native AD. A separate mandatory compiler lane checks a coupled two-rate transfer with transitive aliases and a direct measurement-gain term against a closed form.

With a compiler source that includes the derivative API, run each mode in a fresh process:

python examples/forward_sensitivities.py --backend jax --mode augmented --steps 64
python examples/forward_sensitivities.py --backend jax --mode ad --steps 64

Both modes return the full (3,4) derivative of two final states and one measurement with respect to two rates, gain and initial amplitude, on exactly the same fixed RK4 mesh and float64 precision. The augmented system has ten entries. The comparison uses native forward AD for JAX, native reverse AD for Torch, and explicitly labelled central finite differences for NumPy. First-call and synchronized warm times are separate; no universal cost or stability advantage is assumed.

The raw local receipt retains all 12 fresh-process backend/mesh/mode cases, including Jacobians, source hashes, continuous-reference errors and whole-worker RSS. All six paired derivative matrices agree within rtol=atol=1e-8. On this shared one-core CPU run, the 64-step warm augmented/AD times were 31/37 microseconds for JAX and 50/112 ms for Torch; first calls were approximately 0.69/0.64 s and 0.08/0.11 s respectively. Other local test work was active, each case has only one worker, and methods differentiate this particular small output. These advisory measurements do not select a general sensitivity method or establish a portable speedup. The continuous-reference tolerance scales with fourth-order mesh error; a shared fixed-mesh derivative and a continuous derivative have different error targets.

docs.title: Choosing and configuring a solver
docs.text: ModelCore owns output times and state storage. Deterministic systems use CoreSolver and a method selected by RunConfig. Stochastic reaction networks use DirectSSASolver, ThinningSSASolver, TauLeapingSolver, or AdaptiveTauLeapingSolver, because propensities and stoichiometry have different semantics from an ODE right-hand side. In every case the state array selects the Array-API namespace; choosing JAX instead of NumPy does not select a different numerical method.

docs.title: Deterministic method guide
docs.text:
Method Order Split/operator input Typical use euler 1 None Debugging and first-order reference runs heun 2 None Default non-stiff explicit integration rk4 4 None Accurate fixed-step non-stiff integration dopri5 5 (embedded 4) None Efficient adaptive non-stiff integration imex-euler 1 One implicit-Euler operator factory First-order integration of split systems imex-heun-tr 2 One trapezoidal operator factory Split-step doubling covers explicit and implicit error imex-trbdf2 2 Trapezoidal and BDF2-stage factories Split systems needing stronger damping imex-ark3 3 (embedded 2) One implicit-Euler stage factory Higher-order adaptive split systems implicit-euler 1 Jacobian callable One-linearization approximation with first-order damping trapezoidal 2 Jacobian callable One-linearization, second-order integration bdf2 2 Jacobian callable Uniform, fixed-step, one-linearization integration ros2 2 (embedded 1) Jacobian callable L-stable linearly implicit integration sdirk2 2 Full RHS Jacobian and nonlinear solver L-stable fully nonlinear integration

bdf2 currently requires a uniform output grid and adaptive=False. Its first step uses linearly implicit Euler because no previous state exists yet. The other methods support the built-in adaptive controller, subject to the compiled-control-flow boundary described below.

The linear-multistep design note records the coefficient/history contract, restart rules, and the current no-go decision on exposing BDF3 before variable-step and rejection semantics exist.

docs.title: Known deterministic forcing jumps
docs.text:
For a right-continuous, piecewise-smooth explicit RHS, declare every known jump through RunConfig(forcing_breakpoints=(...)). Euler, Heun, RK4 and Dormand–Prince split fixed/adaptive internal steps at those coordinates. Saved output times remain unchanged; including a jump only in the output grid does not replace this declaration.

import numpy as np
from op_engine import CoreSolver, ModelCore
from op_engine.core_solver import RunConfig

core = ModelCore(1, 1, np.asarray([0.0, 2.0]))
core.set_initial_state(np.ones((1, 1)))
CoreSolver(core).run(
    lambda time, state: np.where(time < 1.0, -state, 0.0 * state),
    config=RunConfig(method="rk4", fixed_max_step=0.125,
                     forcing_breakpoints=(1.0,)),
)
# Final state approximates exp(-1); no extra output row is inserted.

The driver integrates the full duration to each boundary. Incoming RHS stages are capped at its representable left neighbor. Stages starting at a declared jump use a representable right neighbor, ensuring that float32 rounding below a producer's float64 coordinate cannot select the old table value. These adjustments affect RHS evaluation times, not the integrated duration, stored times or state. For declared forcing, first-stage/FSAL cache reuse is disabled throughout the solve, including rejected attempts and replay. Smooth runs with an empty declaration retain their existing kernels and cache behavior.

Times must be finite, strictly increasing and remain distinct/finite in the active float32/float64 state/time precision. Global declarations can extend outside the solve interval. Breakpoints are static metadata, with no state reset, jump impulse, inferred event detection, or gradients with respect to moving jump locations. Callbacks must implement the intended right-continuous regimes and remain smooth enough within each segment for the chosen method.

Functional fixed_explicit_step and adaptive_explicit_step accept the same static declaration. External drivers must clip each step at the next jump; fixed_step_sizes(..., forcing_breakpoints=...) provides a static partition. These kernels adjust stage times but do not shorten the supplied duration. Frozen adaptive replay checks forcing provenance and rejects a mesh that crosses a declared jump; rediscover rather than splitting an accepted replay step. Parameter gradients remain conditional on the frozen mesh and jump times.

The provider merges system.option("forcing_breakpoints") with configured boundaries at each run/preparation, without modifying the reusable engine. This automatically handles op_system time_interpolation: previous tables in flat/PyTree/block fixed runs, prepared execution and adaptive replay. Other deterministic methods and hybrid execution reject declared jumps until their stage/history policies are implemented. Previously the deterministic provider ignored producer declarations, so these unsupported methods now fail clearly. Smooth linear tables publish no jumps and retain their existing behavior.

The implementation follows the known-jump split/cache-refresh principles in Diffrax's controllers and SciML's solver options, with explicit one-sided times for op_system's right-continuous convention.

docs.title: Stochastic reaction networks
docs.text: All stochastic solvers use one reaction contract: the stoichiometric matrix has shape (n_species, n_reactions), while the propensity function returns the state shape with n_reactions replacing n_species on the configured reaction axis.

docs.title: Exact direct SSA
docs.text:
DirectSSASolver implements Gillespie's direct method. It samples one exponential waiting time and one categorical reaction/batch event, applies exactly one stoichiometric update, and repeats. A draw beyond an output boundary is retained rather than discarded, so adding observation times does not alter the simulated path. Zero total propensity is absorbing when no declared future forcing boundary remains.

Use direct SSA as the reference method for low-copy-number networks, rare-event questions, or checking a tau-leaping approximation. Its cost is proportional to the number of individual events, so tau-leaping is usually preferable when populations and firing rates are high.

import numpy as np

from op_engine import DirectSSASolver, ModelCore, NumpySSASampler

times = np.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 41)
core = ModelCore(n_states=2, n_subgroups=1, time_grid=times)
core.set_initial_state(np.asarray([[20.0], [0.0]]))

# A -> B
stoichiometry = np.asarray([[-1], [1]])


def propensity(_time, state):
    return 0.2 * state[0:1]


DirectSSASolver(core, stoichiometry).run(
    propensity,
    NumpySSASampler(seed=2026),
)

The direct method assumes propensities remain constant in time while the state is unchanged, except at explicitly declared forcing boundaries. Across batch cells it samples from the superposed event process; the result is equivalent to independent direct-method trajectories for independent batch cells.

docs.title: Piecewise-constant forcing
docs.text:
Declare every forcing change through DirectSSAConfig.forcing_breakpoints:

from op_engine import DirectSSAConfig, array_namespace

core = ModelCore(n_states=1, n_subgroups=1, time_grid=np.linspace(0.0, 3.0, 13))
core.set_initial_state(np.zeros((1, 1)))


def forced_birth_rate(time, state):
    xp = array_namespace(state)
    rate = 0.0 if time < 1.0 else (3.0 if time < 2.0 else 1.0)
    return xp.full(state.shape, rate, dtype=state.dtype)


DirectSSASolver(core, np.asarray([[1]])).run(
    forced_birth_rate,
    NumpySSASampler(seed=2026),
    config=DirectSSAConfig(forcing_breakpoints=(1.0, 2.0)),
)

If an event would reach or cross a forcing boundary, the solver advances to that boundary without firing, reevaluates the rates, and redraws. Exponential memorylessness makes this exact for piecewise-constant forcing. Zero-rate intervals advance to the next forcing boundary without drawing randomness.

Forcing is right-continuous: the callback must return the new rates at a breakpoint. In an exact event/breakpoint tie, the forcing boundary wins and the old event is discarded. Observation times remain independent of the forcing schedule, even when an observation coincides with a breakpoint.

Breakpoints must be finite real scalars in strictly increasing order. They are snapshotted as an immutable tuple; a global schedule may include times outside the solve interval. Boundaries at the initial time are already reflected in the first evaluation, and the final boundary causes no extra random draw. An omitted or empty schedule preserves ordinary time-homogeneous execution.

The schedule does not freeze or interpolate callback values. All time dependence between boundaries must be constant for this exactness claim; smoothly varying rates require a different waiting-time method. In particular, op_system defaults to linear interpolation of time-indexed parameters, so listing their grid points as breakpoints does not make direct SSA exact for those interpolated rates. An op_system producer can select time_interpolation: previous to hold table values until the next coordinate. The flepimop2 engine provider consumes their published forcing_breakpoints automatically in pure stochastic mode and combines them with any extra boundaries in the engine configuration. This also supports fixed and adaptive tau-leaping. Any additional direct time dependence must still satisfy the chosen solver's exactness conditions.

docs.title: Exact SSA for smooth forcing
docs.text: ThinningSSASolver accepts time-dependent propensities and a user-certified total-rate bound. It samples candidates at the bound rate, then evaluates channel rates at the candidate time to reject or apply one event. See the bounded thinning guide for constant and callback bounds, sampling injection, interval expiry, and a runnable smooth-birth example.

docs.title: Bounded adaptive tau-leaping
docs.text:
Both tau-leaping configurations accept the same forcing_breakpoints schedule as direct SSA. Each leap is capped at the next observation or forcing time, as well as the method's usual step-size limit. The next leap evaluates the right-continuous rates at that boundary. Boundaries count toward the fixed or adaptive method's max_steps guard for the entire output interval; they do not reset it.

For example, the piecewise birth callback above can also use fixed tau-leaping:

from op_engine import NumpyPoissonSampler, TauLeapingConfig, TauLeapingSolver

core = ModelCore(n_states=1, n_subgroups=1, time_grid=np.linspace(0.0, 3.0, 13))
core.set_initial_state(np.zeros((1, 1)))

TauLeapingSolver(core, np.asarray([[1]])).run(
    forced_birth_rate,
    NumpyPoissonSampler(seed=2026),
    config=TauLeapingConfig(max_step=0.1, forcing_breakpoints=(1.0, 2.0)),
)

Adaptive tau-leaping uses these caps for both accepted leaps and rejected proposals. A critical event tied with a forcing boundary is discarded, while noncritical Poisson counts cover the segment ending there. During exact fallback, a pending event survives observation times but is discarded at or beyond the next forcing change. Zero total propensity waits for that change without drawing randomness; without a future boundary it remains absorbing.

Boundary caps keep a leap from using the old rate across a known change. The usual tau-leaping approximation still freezes state-dependent propensities within each leap. Smooth time variation between boundaries also remains an approximation for leaps and is unsupported by adaptive exact fallback. For that fallback, use rates constant in time between declared forcing changes while the state is unchanged.

AdaptiveTauLeapingSolver implements the species-based pre-leap selector of Cao, Gillespie, and Petzold together with their non-negative modified Poisson algorithm. It needs both net stoichiometry and non-negative reactant stoichiometry. They are intentionally separate: net changes cannot reveal catalytic reactants or how many source molecules a reaction consumes.

from op_engine import (
    AdaptiveTauLeapingConfig,
    AdaptiveTauLeapingSolver,
    NumpyPoissonSampler,
    NumpySSASampler,
)

# Net A -> B changes and consumed reactants, respectively.
stoichiometry = np.asarray([[-1], [1]])
reactants = np.asarray([[1], [0]])

solver = AdaptiveTauLeapingSolver(core, stoichiometry, reactants)
solver.run(
    propensity,
    NumpyPoissonSampler(seed=2026),
    NumpySSASampler(seed=2027),
    config=AdaptiveTauLeapingConfig(leap_tolerance=0.03),
)

The non-negativity strategy has three explicit layers:

  1. Pre-leap selection. Species drift and variance from noncritical reactions bound expected and stochastic population changes. The leap_tolerance controls this approximation.
  2. Bounded critical events. A channel is critical when fewer than critical_threshold firings could exhaust a reactant. Across all critical channel/batch events, at most one is selected by the exact-event sampler in a leap. If all active channels are critical, the method is direct SSA.
  3. Post-leap rejection. If noncritical Poisson firings still propose a negative population, the proposal is discarded, the attempted tau is halved, and fresh samples use new deterministic draw indices. No population or firing count is clipped.

When the selected tau is cheaper to execute event by event, exact_fallback_multiplier switches temporarily to direct SSA. Tightening leap_tolerance therefore approaches, and eventually crosses into, the exact reference path on low-count networks.

Per-channel binomial firing was considered but is not used here. Although a binomial draw bounds one channel, independent binomials can still collectively overconsume a reactant shared by several channels. A true coupled-binomial scheme would need a distinct sampling contract. The critical-event bound plus explicit post-leap rejection gives a documented non-negative method without silently changing those reaction dependencies.

docs.title: Fixed-step tau-leaping
docs.text:
Fixed-step explicit tau-leaping approximates the number of firings in each reaction channel over a time interval with an independent Poisson draw. Supply a stoichiometric matrix with shape (n_species, n_reactions) and a propensity function whose reaction axis has length n_reactions:

import numpy as np

from op_engine import (
    ModelCore,
    NumpyPoissonSampler,
    TauLeapingConfig,
    TauLeapingSolver,
)

times = np.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 41)
core = ModelCore(n_states=2, n_subgroups=1, time_grid=times)
core.set_initial_state(np.asarray([[1_000.0], [0.0]]))

# A -> B
stoichiometry = np.asarray([[-1], [1]])


def propensity(_time, state):
    return 0.2 * state[0:1]


solver = TauLeapingSolver(core, stoichiometry)
solver.run(
    propensity,
    NumpyPoissonSampler(seed=2026),
    config=TauLeapingConfig(max_step=0.05),
)

max_step=None takes one leap per output interval. Setting max_step divides each interval into smaller leaps and clips the final leap so that it lands on the requested output time. The propensity is evaluated at the beginning of each leap.

The core solver does not own random-number state. Instead, it receives a PoissonSampler, keeping PRNG details outside the numerical method. A JAX run can use an explicit key and the stable leap index:

key = jax.random.key(2026)


def poisson(mean, step_index):
    return jax.random.poisson(jax.random.fold_in(key, step_index), mean)

This first implementation deliberately rejects a leap that produces a negative population. It neither clips counts nor changes the process silently. Reduce max_step for a better fixed-tau approximation, or use AdaptiveTauLeapingSolver when automatic leap selection and critical-event handling are required.

Tau-leaping is currently an eager execution path: validation reads sampled counts and proposed populations back to Python. JAX arrays stay in their native namespace, but a sampled stochastic trajectory does not provide an ordinary pathwise jax.grad derivative. Differentiable deterministic counterparts can continue to use CoreSolver; gradient estimators for stochastic paths belong at a higher inference/provider layer.

docs.title: Explicit deterministic methods
docs.text:
Euler, Heun, classic RK4, and Dormand--Prince need only an RHS. The default is fixed-step Heun, with one step per output interval:

import numpy as np

from op_engine import CoreSolver, ModelCore
from op_engine.core_solver import AdaptiveConfig, RunConfig

times = np.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 41)
core = ModelCore(n_states=1, n_subgroups=1, time_grid=times)
core.set_initial_state(np.asarray([[1.0]]))


def rhs(_time, state):
    return -0.5 * state


config = RunConfig(
    method="heun",
    adaptive=True,
    adaptive_cfg=AdaptiveConfig(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-9),
)
CoreSolver(core).run(rhs, config=config)

With adaptive=False, every adjacent pair of output times defines one solver step by default. Set fixed_max_step to bound explicit Euler, Heun, RK4, or Dormand--Prince integration steps independently of the output grid:

config = RunConfig(method="rk4", fixed_max_step=0.25)

Each output interval then uses as many full fixed_max_step steps as fit plus a final remainder step that lands exactly on the next output time. Only the requested output states are stored. Output grids aligned with the fixed-step mesh can therefore be made more or less frequent without changing states at shared times. fixed_max_step is incompatible with adaptive=True; adaptive methods use their controller configuration instead.

With adaptive=True, the controller may take multiple internal steps but still stores only the requested output times.

Heun, RK4, and Dormand--Prince share one validated explicit Runge--Kutta tableau kernel. rk4 takes four RHS stages per fixed step. Under adaptivity it uses step doubling to estimate error, so dopri5 is normally the more efficient adaptive choice: its embedded fourth-order formula estimates error using the same seven stages as its fifth-order solution. Dormand--Prince also reuses its final stage as the first stage of the next accepted step (FSAL), including across output-time boundaries.

dopri5, rk45, and dormand-prince select the same canonical method. Dense output is not currently exposed; the solver lands on and stores the requested output times instead of interpolating between accepted internal steps.

docs.title: IMEX methods and operator factories
docs.text:
IMEX methods solve a split system

[ y' = A(t, y)y + F(t, y), ]

where the RHS callable supplies F and an operator factory supplies the implicit part. A resolved operator tuple is either (L, R) or (predictor, L, R), with the core solving L @ y_next = R @ x along the configured operator axis.

Use a StageOperatorFactory whenever the output spacing is non-uniform or adaptive stepping is enabled. The factory receives the attempted full-step size, a stage scale, and StageOperatorContext, so it can rebuild operators for the actual stage time and state.

import numpy as np

from op_engine import CoreSolver, ModelCore, build_diffusion_matrix
from op_engine.core_solver import OperatorSpecs, RunConfig
from op_engine.matrix_ops import (
    StageOperatorContext,
    make_stage_operator_factory,
)

n_cells = 32
dx = 1.0 / n_cells
diffusivity = 0.02
times = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 21)

core = ModelCore(n_states=n_cells, n_subgroups=1, time_grid=times)
core.set_initial_state(np.ones((n_cells, 1)))


def reaction(_time, state):
    return -0.1 * state


def diffusion(ctx: StageOperatorContext):
    return build_diffusion_matrix(
        n_cells,
        dx,
        diffusivity,
        bc="neumann",
        reference=ctx.y,
    )


trapezoidal = make_stage_operator_factory(diffusion, scheme="trapezoidal")
config = RunConfig(
    method="imex-heun-tr",
    operators=OperatorSpecs(default=trapezoidal),
)
CoreSolver(core, operator_axis="state").run(reaction, config=config)

docs.title: Adaptive Heun--trapezoidal error control
docs.text:
Set adaptive=True and supply a timestep-dependent trapezoidal factory for imex-heun-tr. Its estimator compares one complete split step full with two complete half steps refined, including their explicit and implicit stages. Each factory call receives the actual timestep, stage time and candidate state.

The accepted state remains full, with local error estimated by (4/3) * (refined - full). For a smooth second-order problem the refinement difference has cubic leading order; the timestep controller uses exponent -1/3. The factor 4/3 estimates the full-step error. A factor 1/3 would estimate the error of the two-half-step state instead.

This replaces the old explicit-only low/high difference, which could vanish when the explicit RHS was zero even though the implicit time-discretization error was nonzero. Adaptive meshes and results can therefore change, including for mixed systems. Fixed stepping and replay keep the original full-step formula and perform two RHS evaluations and two implicit solves per step. Live adaptive estimation performs six of each per attempted step, including rejected attempts. Static operator pairs remain supported for uniform fixed steps; adaptive runs require a factory so half-step operators are rebuilt.

The required CPU qualification checks pure implicit and mixed scalar decay against exact exponentials, cubic estimator scaling, tolerance refinement, factory stage contexts and replay equivalence. Structured transport checks provide independent matrix-exponential references. These are local truncation error estimates, rather than global accuracy bounds. Trapezoidal integration also retains its usual lack of L-stability. State-dependent or nonsmooth assembly requires an independent convergence check for the actual problem; metadata or a successful controller decision does not qualify it.

Step doubling also supplies implicit error estimates in GSL. An embedded additive pair can reduce estimation cost, as described by ARKODE, but replacing the Heun--trapezoidal stages would change this method's fixed and replay behavior. The existing imex-ark3 provides a separately qualified additive-tableau method. Mesh discovery provenance records the Heun--trapezoidal estimator and the partitions it covers; see replay provenance.

For a non-uniform axis, pass strictly increasing cell-center coordinates and set dx=None:

centers = np.asarray([0.0, 0.08, 0.21, 0.5, 1.0])
operator = build_diffusion_matrix(
    centers.size,
    None,
    diffusivity,
    grid=centers,
    bc="neumann",
)

The no-flux operator is conservative and self-adjoint under the inferred cell-volume weights. It is generally not symmetric in the unweighted Euclidean inner product. Periodic non-uniform grids need an explicit wrap spacing, which cannot be inferred from center coordinates alone, and are rejected.

Use generate_adaptive_grid to create a curvature-weighted point grid from a vectorized profile callable:

from op_engine import generate_adaptive_grid

centers = generate_adaptive_grid(
    lambda x: np.exp(-10.0 * x * x),
    (-1.0, 1.0),
    65,
    smoothing_window=5,
    minimum_spacing=1e-3,
)

The generator returns exactly the requested number of NumPy coordinates, including both interval endpoints. It is eager preprocessing rather than part of the differentiable solve; the resulting static geometry can drive NumPy, JAX, Torch, or another supported Array-API backend. The sampled-data companion is generate_adaptive_grid_from_data.

For imex-trbdf2, provide both stage schemes:

implicit_euler = make_stage_operator_factory(diffusion, scheme="implicit-euler")
config = RunConfig(
    method="imex-trbdf2",
    operators=OperatorSpecs(tr=trapezoidal, bdf2=implicit_euler),
)

imex-ark3 uses the five-stage ARS(4,4,3) additive Runge--Kutta tableau from Ascher, Ruuth, and Spiteri (1997). Its implicit half is L-stable and stiffly accurate. A shared c=1/2 stage supplies a second-order explicit/implicit midpoint estimate, so adaptive error control does not use step doubling.

implicit_euler = make_stage_operator_factory(diffusion, scheme="implicit-euler")
config = RunConfig(
    method="imex-ark3",
    operators=OperatorSpecs(default=implicit_euler),
)

This method always requires a StageOperatorFactory, including on a uniform fixed-step grid. For each non-explicit stage the factory receives the attempted full-step size, the DIRK diagonal coefficient as scale, the actual stage time, and the assembled stage base in StageOperatorContext.y. It must build an implicit-Euler left operator I - dt * scale * A. Predictor tuples are not accepted, and the returned right operator is not applied: the additive kernel has already assembled all previous explicit and implicit stage contributions. The implicit derivative is then recovered from the solved stage equation, which avoids a duplicate callback for A @ y and keeps the method portable across Array-API namespaces.

imex-ars443 and ars443 are aliases for imex-ark3.

The flepimop2 provider can compile typed op_system axis_kernel, jump_integral, advection, and diffusion descriptors into these same factories. Descriptor parsing, axis-type/coordinate resolution, and layout lifting belong to the provider; portable jump assembly follows op_system's public reference semantics, while stepping methods remain in op_engine.

docs.title: Linearly implicit methods
docs.text:
The methods historically named implicit-euler, trapezoidal, and bdf2, as well as the Rosenbrock method, take a Jacobian callable. The callable returns an operator acting along operator_axis:

from op_engine import array_namespace


def jacobian(_time, state):
    xp = array_namespace(state)
    return xp.multiply(xp.eye(state.shape[0], dtype=state.dtype), -0.5)


config = RunConfig(method="ros2", jacobian=jacobian)
CoreSolver(core, operator_axis="state").run(rhs, config=config)

ros2 uses two increment stages and one Jacobian evaluation per attempted step. Both stages solve with the same matrix I - (1 - 1/sqrt(2)) * dt * J; the accepted second-order state and embedded first-order state provide the adaptive error estimate. The coefficient table, formal orders, and controller order are declared together and validated when the module is imported.

Dense Jacobians stay in the state's namespace. SciPy sparse operators are an optional NumPy acceleration path and are not a JAX differentiation path.

The first three methods perform a single linearization; they do not iterate a nonlinear residual to convergence. sdirk2 instead solves each stage through the nonlinear solver contract, with a distinct full flattened Jacobian and explicit convergence diagnostics.

docs.title: Adaptivity and Array-API backends
docs.text:
AdaptiveConfig sets tolerances and attempt limits; DtControllerConfig sets step-size bounds and growth factors. Their static scalar values are validated when the configuration is constructed. Checks that depend on the time grid, state shape, or resolved operators occur when CoreSolver builds its run plan.

Fixed-step explicit, dense IMEX, and dense linearly implicit methods use ordinary Array-API operations. With JAX arrays, those same methods can run under jax.jit and be differentiated with jax.grad; no JAX-specific solver implementation is selected.

The built-in adaptive controller uses eager Python loops and scalar acceptance decisions. It preserves JAX arrays, and an eager jax.grad differentiates the accepted sequence of native steps, but the live controller is not itself JIT-compatible.

For compiled differentiation, record the accepted mesh at representative parameters and replay it:

solver = CoreSolver(reference_core)
solver.run(rhs, config=config)
schedule = solver.last_adaptive_schedule
assert schedule is not None

# Construct a fresh core and solver inside the function being transformed.
solver = CoreSolver(differentiable_core)
diagnostics = solver.replay_adaptive_schedule(rhs, schedule, config=config)

jax.jit(jax.value_and_grad(...)) can trace the replay because its step count and step sizes are static, while array-valued model inputs remain dynamic. The gradient is conditional on that mesh: replay does not differentiate the accept/reject decisions. Refresh the schedule when parameters, tolerances, the method, or other model structure change materially.

For SDIRK2, replay returns array-valued nonlinear diagnostics as part of the compiled result. Inspect diagnostics.require_converged() after execution and discard the replayed state and derivatives if any frozen-mesh stage failed.

A live compiled controller or specialized adjoint implementation can still belong in an external provider and may return a trajectory through ModelCore.apply_trajectory. It should reuse the portable method semantics rather than define a JAX-only numerical method.

See Backend and solve-strategy boundaries for the complete portability contract and the biogeochemical tutorial for a larger IMEX splitting example.

docs.title: Steady States
docs.text: op_engine.steady_state finds an equilibrium y* with rhs(t, y*) = 0, such as the endemic state of an epidemic model, without a long burn-in integration. It uses pseudo-transient continuation: each iteration takes an implicit-Euler step (I/dt - J) delta = rhs(y) and grows dt as the residual falls, so early iterations follow the dynamics and later ones become Newton steps.

docs.title: A first solve
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from op_engine import require_steady_state, steady_state

a = np.array([[-2.0, 1.0], [0.5, -1.0]])
b = np.array([1.0, 2.0])

result = require_steady_state(steady_state(lambda t, y: a @ y + b, np.zeros(2)))
print(result.state, int(result.iterations))

steady_state returns a SteadyStateResult whose diagnostics are arrays: converged, iterations, residual_norm, step_norm, dt, and invariant_drift. require_steady_state raises SteadyStateConvergenceError when the solve did not converge.

docs.title: Epidemic models: sinks and conserved totals
docs.text:
Two features of epidemic models need declaring.

  • Absorbing states. A cumulative counter (deaths, incidence) never reaches a zero derivative while its inflow is positive. Pass it as fixed, by index or mask: it keeps its starting value and is excluded from the convergence test. sink_states(rhs, samples) finds the states no derivative depends on.
  • Conserved totals. When births balance deaths (birth = mu * N), the total population is conserved, so the steady states form a family indexed by it and the Jacobian is singular. Pass the conserved directions as invariants: each row w holds w @ y at its starting value exactly, and the solve stays well posed as dt grows.
  • conserved_quantities(stoichiometry) returns the structural laws of a reaction network, such as S + I + R for a closed SIR.
  • linear_invariants(rhs, samples) also finds totals conserved because rates balance, which births make invisible to the stoichiometry.
from op_engine import linear_invariants, sink_states

beta, gamma, mu, omega = 0.4, 0.1, 1 / (70 * 365), 1 / 365


def sirs(t, y):
    s, i, r, deaths = y
    n = s + i + r
    infection = beta * s * i / n
    return np.array([
        mu * n - infection - mu * s + omega * r,
        infection - (gamma + mu) * i,
        gamma * i - (mu + omega) * r,
        mu * i,
    ])


rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
samples = [rng.uniform(10.0, 3000.0, 4) for _ in range(3)]
sinks = sink_states(sirs, samples)  # [False, False, False, True]
invariants = linear_invariants(sirs, samples, fixed=sinks)  # S + I + R

y0 = np.array([4990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0])
endemic = require_steady_state(
    steady_state(sirs, y0, fixed=sinks, invariants=invariants)
)
print(endemic.state[:3], float(endemic.invariant_drift))

linear_invariants is numerical: a mode decaying more slowly than tol (default 1e-6) times the fastest rate looks conserved, and slow modes limit the accuracy of the rows it returns. When you know an invariant, pass the exact row (here [[1, 1, 1, 0]]) and use linear_invariants to confirm that nothing else is conserved.

For an op_system model, use the compiled RHS. The reaction network gives the structural laws:

from op_system import compile_spec

from op_engine import conserved_quantities, from_compiled_rhs

compiled = compile_spec({
    "kind": "transitions",
    "state": ["S", "I", "R"],
    "transitions": [
        {"name": "infect", "from": "S", "to": "I", "rate": "b * I / (S + I + R)"},
        {"name": "recover", "from": "I", "to": "R", "rate": "g"},
        {"name": "wane", "from": "R", "to": "S", "rate": "w"},
    ],
})
params = {"b": 0.4, "g": 0.1, "w": 0.01}
network = from_compiled_rhs(compiled, params)
closed = conserved_quantities(network.stoichiometry)  # one row: S + I + R


def rhs(t, y):
    return np.asarray(compiled.eval_fn(t, y, **params))


sirs_state = require_steady_state(
    steady_state(rhs, np.array([990.0, 10.0, 0.0]), invariants=closed)
).state

docs.title: Convergence
docs.text:
A solve converges when two conditions hold, with the scale atol + |y| per state:

  • the scaled residual RMS is at most residual_tol;
  • the Newton correction, scaled the same way, is at most step_tol.

The second condition matters for slowly decaying modes. Near a steady state the error is about residual / rate, so a residual of 1e-9 along a mode decaying at 1e-7 per day still leaves an error of about 1e-2. The Newton correction measures that error directly, and the final correction is applied to the returned state.

Pseudo-transient continuation converges to a steady state: started next to an unstable one, such as the disease-free state, it can stop there. The dt schedule holds the step through bounded residual growth, as it does while an epidemic takes off. A small dt0 (the default is 1 time unit) lets the iterates follow the dynamics toward a stable equilibrium. Candidates with non-finite states or residuals, or with scaled or unscaled residual growth above max_growth, are rejected: the previous state and residual are retained, and dt is halved for the next attempt. Rejections count toward max_iterations; a smaller dt0 or a short time integration can provide a better starting point if the budget is insufficient. Warm starts from a nearby solution converge fastest; raise dt0 for those.

For compartment populations or concentrations, pass nonnegative=True to reject negative candidates, including the final Newton correction. A boolean mask constrains selected states when the model also contains signed variables:

result = steady_state(rhs, y0, invariants=totals, nonnegative=True)

This guard is especially useful for fast take-off from a seeded disease-free state, where a large pseudo-time step can overshoot into negative populations or select the unstable equilibrium. Rejected steps preserve the invariant totals; the solver does not clip states. Signs remain unrestricted by default. The guard helps follow a physical trajectory but cannot guarantee convergence to a particular equilibrium or avoid an iteration limit.

SteadyStateConfig collects the controls: dt0, dt_max, min_growth, max_growth, max_iterations, residual_tol, step_tol, and atol. The default tolerances assume double precision.

The safeguard retains pseudo-transient continuation for the coupled system. Brent's method and bisection need a scalar sign-changing bracket, which a general RHS does not provide. The existing curvature-weighted grid utilities are spatial preprocessing tools. For background on constraints and step control, see projected pseudo-transient continuation and PETSc's pseudo-time step verification.

docs.title: JAX: jit and vmap
docs.text:
Pass an automatic-differentiation Jacobian and loop=jax.lax.fori_loop. The loop compiles the iteration once, where the default Python loop would unroll max_iterations copies of it. Invariants and the fixed mask are setup data, so build them outside the traced function.

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

from op_engine import SteadyStateConfig

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)
total = np.ones((1, 3))


def endemic_state(beta, y0):
    def rhs(t, y):
        s, i, r = y[0], y[1], y[2]
        n = s + i + r
        return jnp.stack([
            mu * n - beta * s * i / n - mu * s + omega * r,
            beta * s * i / n - (gamma + mu) * i,
            gamma * i - (mu + omega) * r,
        ])

    result = steady_state(
        rhs,
        y0,
        jacobian=lambda t, y: jax.jacfwd(lambda z: rhs(t, z))(y),
        invariants=total,
        config=SteadyStateConfig(max_iterations=60),
        loop=jax.lax.fori_loop,
    )
    return result.state, result.converged


states, converged = jax.jit(jax.vmap(endemic_state, in_axes=(0, None)))(
    jnp.array([0.3, 0.4, 0.5]), jnp.array([4990.0, 10.0, 0.0])
)

Without a jacobian, steady_state uses forward differences, which cost one RHS evaluation per state per iteration.

docs.title: Optional compiled Torch sequential loops
docs.text:
The Torch adapter is an explicit CPU execution choice. It reuses the native fixed explicit step kernels through the existing LoopAdapter registry and captures a bounded sequential loop with fullgraph Inductor. vmap is not a substitute for this dependency between time steps. Ordinary solver defaults stay fixed_loop="unroll"; importing op_engine or this adapter module does not import Torch.

import torch
from op_engine import array_namespace
from op_engine.loop_ops import register_loop_adapter
from op_engine.torch_loop import torch_compile_loop_adapter

adapter = torch_compile_loop_adapter(max_steps=128, max_elements=65_536)
register_loop_adapter(array_namespace(torch.ones(1)).__name__, adapter)
# Explicitly select RunConfig(fixed_loop="scan", fixed_max_step=...).

docs.title: Supported boundary
docs.text:
Property Qualified contract Torch CPU 2.14.1; the factory requires >=2.14. Eager >=2.6 remains separate. Arithmetic Homogeneous native CPU float32 or float64. No host/device transfer inside the adapter. Methods Fixed Euler, Heun, RK4, Dormand–Prince; original full-step kernels and FSAL carry. Trees Tensor/None leaves in standard tuple/list/dict carry and outputs; native tensor input leaves with a common leading dimension. Carry/output structure, shapes, dtype and device stay fixed. Body Functional native numerical operations; no input mutation or side effects. Independent input values remain runtime values. Bounds Positive static scan length, default/hard maximum 128; configurable input+carry+stacked-output element bound, default 65,536 and hard maximum 1,048,576. These are not process RSS or internal RHS allocation caps. Derivatives First reverse-mode gradients of the qualified consumers, including parameters and initial states. Checkpoint Not supplied; explicitly requested checkpointing raises in the consumer. Empty loops Consumers skip an empty tail after their first bootstrap step. No generic unknown-output shape inference for zero-length scans. Device CPU only. CuPy, Torch and JAX GPU work is separately on hold pending the workstation session.

Adaptive policy differentiation, implicit replay kernels, higher derivatives, mixed precision, custom pytree registrations, sparse states, GPU execution, estimator training and shared simulator/estimator graphs are outside this qualification. Separately simulated training banks remain valid consumers. For scalar compiler/observable paths, use the merged op_system prerequisite PR #341; the runtime callable boundary and minimum-Torch gradient fixes are part of that reviewed source.

The adapter statically unrolls a bounded sequential loop into a native graph. Its graph size and cold compilation grow with the step count. It does not have the constant-size graph property of JAX's lax.scan; long meshes should continue using the separately qualified JAX path or eager execution as appropriate. Changing a method, body structure, shape, dtype or static grid may recompile. Each explicit adapter owns a distinct compiler code identity, avoiding a shared factory specialization budget. Torch's own compiler caches and generated code still contribute to process memory.

docs.title: Required compilation and errors
docs.text:
fullgraph=True, dynamic=False, and the Inductor backend are selected explicitly. Graph breaks and unsupported numerical bodies raise rather than returning an eager fallback. The raw body also rejects disabled compilation. Qualification exercises a real graph break even with global error suppression, and tests the startup TORCH_COMPILE_DISABLE switch in a fresh process. It does not treat FX inspection or a Python-only backend as native acceleration. Unsupported versions, bounds, leaves, devices and dtypes fail explicitly. The package makes no automatic backend/default selection based on these results.

# Install CPU Torch 2.14.1 explicitly, then require zero skipped cases:
python scripts/qualify_backend.py torch --torch-compile

The dedicated hosted job uses the CPU wheel index. Tests include independently written stability-polynomial values/gradients for all four methods and both precisions, dynamic parameter changes, stored/final-only results, nested observation output trees, optional FSAL carry, positive-length boundaries, oversized output/carry errors and disabled/broken compilation. Minimum-Torch CI also checks that compiled support is explicitly rejected without affecting eager state/gradient checks.

docs.title: Consumer measurements
docs.text:
The complete receipt retains 32 serial fresh workers: two consumers × 8/32 steps × float32/64 × eager/compiled × two repetitions, reversing mode order in the second repetition. Twenty-five warm calls per phase follow independent discrete RK4 value/gradient checks for two parameter sets. The actual observation consumer is the public op_infer scalar fixture; the core case has two scalar states. All 32 workers passed, with native Inductor kernels and no recorded graph breaks in each compiled worker.

The host was an Intel Core Ultra 7 265U, Python 3.12.14, Torch 2.14.1+cpu, NumPy 2.5.4 and array-api-compat 1.15.0. Workers used one pinned CPU, one OpenBLAS/OMP/compiler thread and separate empty compiler caches. These bounded toy cases do not establish results across larger models or different hardware.

Ratios are eager latency divided by compiled latency, using the median of the two process medians; values below one indicate a regression. First forward and backward are separate process medians in seconds. Warm value+gradient includes its forward call.

Consumer Steps Precision Warm forward ratio Warm value+gradient ratio First forward / backward (s) core 8 float32 0.86× 1.14× 10.8 / 8.1 core 8 float64 1.37× 1.74× 10.3 / 8.6 core 32 float32 3.70× 4.50× 27.8 / 29.2 core 32 float64 3.67× 4.33× 31.7 / 41.3 observations 8 float32 2.22× 2.34× 19.9 / 10.8 observations 8 float64 2.13× 2.45× 24.7 / 10.6 observations 32 float32 7.40× 8.63× 55.3 / 49.4 observations 32 float64 6.73× 7.83× 55.3 / 33.5

Compiled process peak RSS was 441–587 MiB. Eight additional fresh ordinary eager memory controls, one per condition and all passing, used 249–274 MiB. The primary timing workers import compiler diagnostic modules in both modes; their instrumented eager RSS of 317–341 MiB must not be presented as ordinary eager memory. The extra controls omit those unused imports and remain separate from the timing ratios. RSS includes imports/compiler state and excludes child compiler processes; it is distinct from output-array size or a hard memory cap.

The smallest core float32 warm forward regresses, and cold forward/backward costs and compiler memory can outweigh repeated-call savings. Retain explicit opt-in and existing eager defaults. These two-replicate observations support bounded engineering decisions, not general timing CI thresholds, GPU or estimator-training claims. Source snapshots, hashes, raw samples, compiler diagnostics, stderr, and the eight memory controls are in the receipt; the summary records the protocol limits. Only lint comments changed in the adapter during collection; all exact snapshots and their identical executable AST digest are retained.

To rerun, extract reproduction_files from the gzip JSON into a new directory. Install the receipt’s Python/backend versions in a separate CPU environment and provide the engine, compiler and op_infer checkouts to the relocatable coordinator:

python reproduce.py --python /path/to/cpu-env/bin/python \
    --engine-checkout /path/to/op_engine --system-checkout /path/to/op_system \
    --infer-checkout /path/to/op_infer --output /path/to/new-results

The archived plain-eager worker runs the separate memory control by selecting --mode unroll; it deliberately omits unused compiler-diagnostic imports. Feasibility timings are not pooled into this comparison.
